newsitem.title: USA: IMF concerned by emerging nations' yen bond issues.
newsitem.headline: IMF concerned by emerging nations' yen bond issues.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday warned emerging market borrowers and retail investors in Germany and Japan about the risks posed by the mushrooming issuance of yen- and mark-denominated bonds.
The sharp rise in such issues has been led by countries from Latin America, although some East European nations have also been active borrowers.

"The rapid increase ... raises questions regarding the ability of some emerging market countries to manage currency exposures prudently," IMF staff said in their annual report of international capital markets.
"It also puts into question the ability of retail investors to assess adequately sovereign credit risk," they said.
Faced with very low interest rates on Japanese government bonds, Japanese retail investors have snapped up issues by developing countries.

But the IMF report questioned whether they fully understand the risks involved, noting that ratings agencies in Japan have consistently given developing countries higher ratings than have their counterparts in the United States.

"Of particular interest is the case of the National Bank of Hungary, a long-time issuer in the Samurai and Euroyen markets despite having a subinvestment grade rating from both Moody's (Investors Service) and S & P (Standard and Poor's)," the report said.
The IMF staff also questioned whether emerging market borrowers in the yen and mark bond markets fully understood the currency risk they face.
The report cited concerns that "issuers have underestimated the potential exchange rate risk under the attraction of the very low nominal (Japanese) interest rates."
"The risks inherent in foreign-currency denominated debt were most acutely demonstrated by the Mexican financial crisis," the IMF report said.
Countries that have been the biggest borrowers in these markets include Argentina, which issued $1.7 billion worth of yen paper last year, and Mexico, with $1.6 billion.
Other big borrowers include Brazil, Colombia, Hungary, Turkey and Romania.
